milestones.title: samplers from uniform numbers
milestones.task: Write sample_exponential(rng, rate), sample_categorical(rng, probs), box_muller(rng) returning a pair, and rejection_sample(rng, density, bound, n) returning (samples, tries). Each uses exactly the number of rng.random() calls stated in its docstring, in the stated order, so that a scripted source can test it.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py 1 shows this milestone as ✔. It checks hand answers on scripted uniforms (the exponential at u = 0.5, the categorical at the boundaries 0.5, 0.8 and 0.999999, zero-probability entries, the rounding fallback, Box–Muller at 0.5 and 0.25, a zero draw, and a two-proposal rejection run), and then, on three seeds of 20,000 draws, the exponential mean and tail, the categorical frequencies, the Gaussian mean, variance, 95% interval and independence of the pair, and the Beta(2, 2) mean, variance and acceptance rate of rejection sampling.
milestones.explain:
A computer has one primitive source of randomness: a pseudo-random number generator that, from a seed, produces a long deterministic sequence that behaves like independent draws from the uniform distribution on [0, 1) (chapter 4 on seeds). Every other distribution is a transformation of those numbers. Four transformations cover most needs.

Inverse-cdf sampling. The cdf F(x) = P(X ≤ x) maps a value to a probability. Draw u uniformly in [0, 1) and return x = F−1(u). Then P(x ≤ a) = P(F−1(U) ≤ a) = P(U ≤ F(a)) = F(a), which is exactly the right distribution. For the exponential with rate λ (waiting times; mean 1/λ), F(x) = 1 − e−λx, which inverts to x = −ln(1 − u)/λ. With λ = 2 and u = 0.5 the answer is ln 2 / 2 = 0.3466, a number the check computes by hand before it samples anything.

Categorical draws. For a distribution over a few outcomes the cdf is a staircase of running totals, and inversion becomes: walk along the totals until you pass u. This is how a token is drawn from a softmax output.

Box–Muller. The Gaussian cdf has no closed-form inverse, so a different change of variables is used. Two independent standard Gaussians, viewed in the plane, have a rotationally symmetric joint density; the squared distance from the origin, R2, then has an exponential distribution with mean 2 and the angle is uniform. Sampling those two with u1 and u2 gives z1 = √(−2 ln u1) cos(2πu2) and z2 = √(−2 ln u1) sin(2πu2). Python's random.random() can return exactly 0.0 but never 1.0, so the lab uses 1 − random() inside the logarithm, which is never 0.

Rejection sampling. When even a pdf is awkward to invert, propose a point x uniformly on [0, 1] and a height u, and keep x if u < f(x)/M, where M is any bound on the density. The kept points have density f. Each proposal succeeds with probability 1/M (the density integrates to 1 and the box has area M), so the method costs M proposals per sample, which is cheap for a gentle density and ruinous for a spiky one. The script runs all four, plus a deliberately narrow density:

import math
import random
from solution import sample_exponential, sample_categorical, box_muller, rejection_sample

rng = random.Random(7)
N = 100_000
xs = [sample_exponential(rng, 2.0) for _ in range(N)]
print(f"exponential(rate 2): mean {sum(xs) / N:.4f} (exact 0.5), P(X > 1) {sum(x > 1 for x in xs) / N:.4f} (exact {math.exp(-2):.4f})")

probs = [0.5, 0.3, 0.15, 0.05]
draws = [sample_categorical(rng, probs) for _ in range(N)]
print("categorical frequencies:", [round(draws.count(i) / N, 4) for i in range(4)], "target", probs)

zs = [z for _ in range(N // 2) for z in box_muller(rng)]
mean = sum(zs) / len(zs)
var = sum((z - mean) ** 2 for z in zs) / len(zs)
print(f"Box-Muller: mean {mean:.4f}, variance {var:.4f}, P(|Z| < 1.96) {sum(abs(z) < 1.96 for z in zs) / len(zs):.4f} (exact 0.9500)")

samples, tries = rejection_sample(rng, lambda x: 6 * x * (1 - x), 1.5, 50_000)
print(f"rejection (6x(1-x)): mean {sum(samples) / len(samples):.4f} (exact 0.5), acceptance {len(samples) / tries:.3f} (exact {1 / 1.5:.3f})")
narrow = lambda x: 10.0 if 0.45 <= x <= 0.55 else 0.0
samples, tries = rejection_sample(rng, narrow, 10.0, 5_000)
print(f"rejection (a bump of width 0.1): acceptance {len(samples) / tries:.3f}, so {tries / len(samples):.1f} proposals per sample")
exponential(rate 2): mean 0.4978 (exact 0.5), P(X > 1) 0.1348 (exact 0.1353)
categorical frequencies: [0.5008, 0.2971, 0.1512, 0.0509] target [0.5, 0.3, 0.15, 0.05]
Box-Muller: mean -0.0001, variance 1.0031, P(|Z| < 1.96) 0.9500 (exact 0.9500)
rejection (6x(1-x)): mean 0.4998 (exact 0.5), acceptance 0.666 (exact 0.667)
rejection (a bump of width 0.1): acceptance 0.099, so 10.1 proposals per sample

Each estimate is within sampling error of the exact value (the check sets that tolerance at five standard errors). The last line shows the cost: a bump of width 0.1 is accepted one time in ten, and the method collapses in high dimensions, where the box is astronomically larger than the density. Production code uses these ideas through a library (numpy.random.Generator has all of them, vectorised), but the categorical draw is worth owning: it is the last line of every text generator.

Common misconception

"Whether the walk stops at u < total or u <= total cannot matter, because u is almost never exactly equal to a total." It matters at the edges. random() can return exactly 0.0, and with <= an outcome with probability 0 at the front of the list would be selected by it: a token the model said was impossible. With the strict <, a zero-probability entry never wins, because its running total does not rise above the one before it. The check has a case for exactly this, with u = 0 and u = 0.5.

milestones.title: likelihoods and maximum-likelihood fits
milestones.task: Write bernoulli_loglik(heads, n, theta), gaussian_loglik(xs, mu, sigma), poisson_loglik(counts, lam) (use math.lgamma(k + 1) for ln k!), gaussian_mle(xs, ddof=0) returning (mean, variance), poisson_mle(counts) and categorical_mle(counts). Raise ValueError for empty data and all-zero counts.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py 2 shows this milestone as ✔. It checks hand values for each log-likelihood (including −916.30 for 1,050 heads in 1,500 flips and the θ = 0, 1 edge cases), the sharpening ratios 0.806, 0.115 and 4.2 × 10−10, the MLEs on small examples and their errors, six seeds of random data on which every MLE must beat its neighbours (and the maximum-likelihood identity above), and a 20,000-repeat simulation of the variance bias at n = 3.
milestones.explain:
Chapter 13's central move is to describe a model as assigning a probability to the data, and to choose parameters that make the observed data as probable as possible. The likelihood L(θ) is the probability of the observed data as a function of the parameter θ; the maximum-likelihood estimate (MLE) is the θ that maximises it. For n independent observations, L is a product of n probabilities, each below 1, so it shrinks towards zero faster than a computer can represent. The remedy is to work with the logarithm: ln L is a sum, it has its maximum at the same θ, and it is what every framework computes. The function you write first makes the problem concrete.

import math
import random
from solution import bernoulli_loglik, gaussian_mle

print("how sharply do the data speak? L(0.6) / L(best) for a coin that came up 70% heads")
for heads, n in ((7, 10), (70, 100), (700, 1000)):
    ratio = math.exp(bernoulli_loglik(heads, n, 0.6) - bernoulli_loglik(heads, n, heads / n))
    print(f"  {heads:3d} heads in {n:4d} flips: {ratio:.3e}")

ll = bernoulli_loglik(1050, 1500, 0.7)
print(f"\n1,500 flips, 1,050 heads, theta = 0.7: log-likelihood {ll:.2f}, but exp of it is {math.exp(ll)}")

rng = random.Random(11)
reps = 20000
print("\naverage variance estimate over 20,000 samples of n points from N(0, 4)")
print(f"{'n':>3} {'divide by n':>12} {'divide by n-1':>14} {'(n-1)/n * 4':>12}")
for n in (3, 5, 10):
    a = b = 0.0
    for _ in range(reps):
        xs = [rng.gauss(0.0, 2.0) for _ in range(n)]
        a += gaussian_mle(xs)[1]
        b += gaussian_mle(xs, ddof=1)[1]
    print(f"{n:>3} {a / reps:12.3f} {b / reps:14.3f} {(n - 1) / n * 4:12.3f}")
how sharply do the data speak? L(0.6) / L(best) for a coin that came up 70% heads
    7 heads in   10 flips: 8.057e-01
   70 heads in  100 flips: 1.153e-01
  700 heads in 1000 flips: 4.158e-10

1,500 flips, 1,050 heads, theta = 0.7: log-likelihood -916.30, but exp of it is 0.0

average variance estimate over 20,000 samples of n points from N(0, 4)
  n  divide by n  divide by n-1  (n-1)/n * 4
  3        2.654          3.981        2.667
  5        3.226          4.032        3.200
 10        3.577          3.974        3.600

Three lessons sit in that output. The likelihood curve sharpens with data: with 10 flips, θ = 0.6 is 81% as likely as the best value, so the data hardly tell them apart; with 1,000 flips it is one in 2.4 billion. The likelihood of 1,500 flips underflows to exactly 0.0 although its logarithm, −916.30, is an ordinary number, so a program that multiplied probabilities would see every θ tie. And the last table is about honesty of estimators: the MLE of a variance divides by n, and is systematically too small, because the residuals are measured from a mean fitted to the same data. For n = 3 the average is two-thirds of the truth; dividing by n − 1 (Bessel's correction) removes the bias. Your gaussian_mle takes a ddof argument so both are available.

The likelihoods and estimators you need are short. For h heads in n flips, ln L(θ) = h ln θ + (n − h) ln(1 − θ), and setting its derivative h/θ − (n − h)/(1 − θ) to zero gives θ = h/n. For Gaussian data, ln L(μ, σ) = −(n/2) ln(2πσ2) − ∑(xi − μ)2/(2σ2), maximised by the sample mean and, for σ2, the mean squared deviation. For Poisson counts ki (events per interval, such as requests per second), ln L(λ) = ∑(ki ln λ − λ − ln ki!), maximised by the mean count. For a categorical variable, the MLE is the observed frequency of each outcome (with a Lagrange multiplier to keep the probabilities summing to 1). In every case, the maximum-likelihood estimate of a probability is a frequency and of a mean is an average, which is reassuring; the work of the milestone is getting the logarithms and the edge cases right.

The edge cases are the part that bites. A probability of exactly 0 for an outcome that did not occur contributes 0 · ln 0, which is defined as 0 here; for an outcome that did occur it makes the data impossible and the log-likelihood −∞. The check also verifies that your MLE really is a maximum, by comparing its log-likelihood with its neighbours on random data, and uses a neat identity: at the Gaussian MLE the squared-error term equals exactly n/2, so the maximum log-likelihood is −(n/2)(ln(2πσ̂2) + 1).

milestones.title: a line fitted by gradient descent on the NLL
milestones.task: Write line_nll(params, xs, ys) returning (nll, [d/dw, d/db, d/ds]) with sums over the data; least_squares(xs, ys) returning (w, b); and fit_line(xs, ys, lr=0.1, steps=1500) returning the final [w, b, s].
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py 3 shows this milestone as ✔. It checks the hand NLL and gradient values above, your gradients against central differences on five random problems, least_squares against an independent solution of the normal equations by Cramer's rule, and, on three datasets, that fit_line reaches the least-squares slope and intercept within 0.001, that exp(s) equals the root-mean-square residual within 0.001, that the result is close to the truth the data were made with, and that the parameters stay finite.
milestones.explain:
Chapter 13's headline result is that squared error is maximum likelihood under Gaussian noise. This milestone proves it numerically, with a model that also learns how noisy the data are. The model is y = wx + b + ε with ε ∼ N(0, σ2). It has three parameters, and to keep σ positive without constraints the code optimises its logarithm, s = ln σ, so that σ2 = e2s. With the residual ri = yi − (wxi + b), the negative log-likelihood is

NLL(w, b, s) = ∑i [ ½ ln(2πσ2) + ri2 / (2σ2) ].

Differentiate by the chain rule (chapter 8). Since ∂ri/∂w = −xi and ∂ri/∂b = −1,

∂NLL/∂w = −∑ ri xi / σ2,    ∂NLL/∂b = −∑ ri / σ2,    ∂NLL/∂s = ∑ (1 − ri2 / σ2).

The first two are the least-squares gradient divided by σ2: the noise level only rescales them, which is why you can fix σ = 1 when fitting weights. The third is new, and its zero is the answer to "how noisy is the data?": 1 = (1/n) ∑ ri2/σ2, so σ2 is the mean squared residual. check.py verifies your three formulas against central differences of your own NLL at random points, as in Lab 2, plus the hand example in the docstring: for the two points (0, 1) and (1, 3), the gradient at (0, 0, 0) is [−3, −4, −8].

Then fit it two ways. least_squares is the closed form from the normal equations: the slope is cov(x, y)/var(x) and the intercept makes the line pass through the point of means. fit_line runs gradient descent on the mean NLL from (0, 0, 0), with learning rate 0.1 and 1,500 steps; the gradient of the mean is the summed gradient divided by n, which keeps the step size independent of the data size and is why the sums in line_nll must be divided by n inside fit_line.

import math
from solution import make_line_data, line_nll, least_squares, fit_line

xs, ys = make_line_data(13, n=100)                       # y = 2x + 1 + noise with sd 0.7
w, b = least_squares(xs, ys)
rms = math.sqrt(sum((y - (w * x + b)) ** 2 for x, y in zip(xs, ys)) / len(xs))
print(f"least squares      : slope {w:.4f}, intercept {b:.4f}, rms residual {rms:.4f}")
for steps in (10, 30, 100, 1500):
    wf, bf, sf = fit_line(xs, ys, steps=steps)
    print(f"gradient descent, {steps:4d} steps: slope {wf:.4f}, intercept {bf:.4f}, sigma {math.exp(sf):.4f}, mean NLL {line_nll([wf, bf, sf], xs, ys)[0] / len(xs):.4f}")
least squares      : slope 1.9802, intercept 1.0750, rms residual 0.7014
gradient descent,   10 steps: slope 0.6932, intercept 0.3078, sigma 1.8897, mean NLL 1.9764
gradient descent,   30 steps: slope 1.5608, intercept 0.7600, sigma 1.1027, mean NLL 1.3431
gradient descent,  100 steps: slope 1.9802, intercept 1.0750, sigma 0.7014, mean NLL 1.0643
gradient descent, 1500 steps: slope 1.9802, intercept 1.0750, sigma 0.7014, mean NLL 1.0643

Descent starts with a large noise estimate (sigma 1.89 after ten steps, as the residuals of a bad line are large), shrinks it as the line improves, and by step 100 agrees with least squares to four decimals: slope 1.9802, intercept 1.0750, and a fitted σ of 0.7014, which is exactly the root-mean-square residual printed above it. The data were made with slope 2, intercept 1 and noise 0.7; 100 points recover them to within sampling error. Two routes, one answer, which is the content of the sentence "least squares is maximum likelihood".

milestones.title: a stable log-softmax and its gradient
milestones.task: Write logsumexp(zs) (raise ValueError for an empty list), log_softmax(zs), softmax(zs) (exponentiate the log-softmax), cross_entropy(logits, target) and cross_entropy_grad(logits, target). Do not modify the list you are given.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py 4 shows this milestone as ✔. It checks hand answers (softmax of 1000, 1001, 1002; log-softmax of [0, −200]; a loss of exactly 200 for a confident mistake; very negative logits; −∞ masks; a single class; an extreme gap of 10308), the gradient [−0.3348, 0.2447, 0.0900], and eight random problems for agreement with the textbook formula on moderate logits, shift invariance by ±thousands, probabilities summing to 1, and the gradient against central differences of your own loss.
milestones.explain:
The softmax turns scores z1, …, zK (the logits) into probabilities pi = ezi / ∑j ezj. Transcribed literally, it breaks on large inputs: math.exp(1000) overflows (Python raises OverflowError; NumPy returns inf and then nan), and logits in the hundreds are normal in practice. The fix rests on one fact. Softmax does not change when you add the same constant c to every logit, because ez+c = ecez and the factor ec cancels from numerator and denominator. Choose c = −max(z) and the largest exponent becomes e0 = 1: nothing can overflow, and the denominator is at least 1.

The same shift gives the log-sum-exp that anchors everything else: logsumexp(z) = ln ∑j ezj = m + ln ∑j ezj − m with m = max(z). From it, ln pi = zi − logsumexp(z): the log-softmax, computed without ever forming a probability. That matters for the second hazard, underflow. A probability like e−800 is below the smallest positive float and becomes exactly 0, and then the loss −ln p is −ln 0 = ∞. The log-softmax of the same logits is a perfectly ordinary −800. Cross-entropy is then a lookup, loss = −log_softmax(z)[target], and this is why every framework fuses softmax and cross-entropy into one function that takes logits.

import math
from solution import softmax, log_softmax, cross_entropy

def naive_softmax(z):
    e = [math.exp(v) for v in z]
    return [v / sum(e) for v in e]

for z in ([1000.0, 1001.0, 1002.0], [0.0, -800.0]):
    print("logits", z)
    try:
        p = naive_softmax(z)
        print("  naive softmax      :", p)
        print("  log of the naive   :", [math.log(v) for v in p])
    except (OverflowError, ValueError) as e:
        print(f"  naive pipeline     : {type(e).__name__}: {e}")
    print("  stable softmax     :", [round(p, 6) for p in softmax(z)])
    print("  stable log_softmax :", [round(v, 6) for v in log_softmax(z)])
print("\ncross-entropy of a confident mistake: logits [0, 200], true class 0 ->", cross_entropy([0.0, 200.0], 0))
logits [1000.0, 1001.0, 1002.0]
  naive pipeline     : OverflowError: math range error
  stable softmax     : [0.090031, 0.244728, 0.665241]
  stable log_softmax : [-2.407606, -1.407606, -0.407606]
logits [0.0, -800.0]
  naive softmax      : [1.0, 0.0]
  naive pipeline     : ValueError: expected a positive input, got 0.0
  stable softmax     : [1.0, 0.0]
  stable log_softmax : [0.0, -800.0]

cross-entropy of a confident mistake: logits [0, 200], true class 0 -> 200.0

The naive pipeline fails in two different ways on the two inputs (an overflow in the exponential, and a log of an underflowed zero), and the stable pair handles both. The same holds at the other extreme: a confident mistake, with the true class 200 logits below the winner, costs a loss of exactly 200, not infinity.

Two more pieces finish the milestone. Masking: attention and decoding code sets the logits of forbidden options to −∞, so logsumexp must cope with −∞ entries (their exponential is a clean 0), and with a list that is all −∞ (where z - max would be −∞ − (−∞) = nan; the answer is −∞). The gradient: differentiate the loss L = −zt + logsumexp(z) with respect to zi. The first term contributes −1 when i = t; the second contributes ezi/∑ezj = pi. So

∂L/∂zi = pi − [i = t],

the predicted probabilities minus the one-hot target. This is the result Lab 2 confirmed through its autograd engine, and it is why training a classifier is so well behaved: the gradient is bounded between −1 and 1 however wrong the prediction is. For logits (2, 1, 0) and target 0 it is (−0.335, 0.245, 0.090), and it sums to 0.

milestones.title: temperature, entropy and truncation
milestones.task: Write softmax_t(logits, temperature), entropy(p, base=2.0), perplexity(p, base=2.0), top_k(p, k), top_p(p, nucleus) and sample_token(rng, logits, temperature=1.0, k=None, p=None). Ties in top-k and top-p go to the lower index. The given normalise helper rescales a list to sum to 1.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py 5 shows this milestone as ✔. It checks the chapter figures (the top probability at T = 1, 0.5, 2; the entropy at six temperatures; top-k with k = 3; top-p at 0.9, 0.85, 0.01 and 1.0), stability at T = 0.001 and 106, errors for T ≤ 0, k < 1 and p outside (0, 1], entropy rising with T, entropy of uniform and one-hot distributions, that perplexity does not depend on the unit, on random distributions that the top-p set reaches the nucleus, is the smallest such set and is made of the most probable tokens, sample_token on scripted uniforms, and, on 20,000 draws, the frequencies of a draw at T = 0.8 with k = 3 and p = 0.95.
milestones.explain:
A language model's last layer produces one logit per vocabulary entry. To generate text you choose a token from the softmax of those logits, and three controls shape the choice (A2, chapter 15 treats them as decoding strategies; here you build the arithmetic). Temperature T divides the logits before the softmax: pi = softmax(z/T)i. For T below 1 the largest logits pull further ahead and the distribution sharpens; for T above 1 it flattens; as T tends to 0 it approaches the arg-max, and as T grows the logits stop mattering and it tends to uniform. Top-k keeps only the k most probable tokens, zeroes the rest and renormalises. Top-p (nucleus sampling; Holtzman et al., 2019, The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration) keeps the smallest set of most probable tokens whose probabilities add up to at least p, a set whose size adapts to how confident the model is: two tokens when the model is sure, hundreds when it is not.

To describe how much choice is left, chapter 14 uses the entropy H(p) = −∑ pi log pi, the average surprise in bits when the logarithm has base 2, and the perplexity 2H, the effective number of equally likely options. A uniform distribution over 8 tokens has entropy 3 bits and perplexity 8; a distribution that puts all its mass on one token has entropy 0 and perplexity 1. Terms with pi = 0 contribute nothing (0 log 0 = 0), which the code has to say explicitly. The figure sweeps the temperature on the chapter's six example logits.

import random
from solution import LOGITS, TOKENS, softmax_t, entropy, perplexity, top_k, top_p, sample_token

print(f"{'T':>6} {'max prob':>9} {'entropy (bits)':>15} {'perplexity':>11}")
for T in (0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 5.0, 100.0):
    p = softmax_t(LOGITS, T)
    print(f"{T:6} {max(p):9.3f} {entropy(p):15.3f} {perplexity(p):11.2f}")

p = softmax_t(LOGITS, 1.0)
print("\n" + " " * 16 + " ".join(f"{t:>5}" for t in TOKENS))
for name, q in (("T = 1", p), ("top-k, k = 3", top_k(p, 3)), ("top-p, 0.9", top_p(p, 0.9))):
    print(f"{name:<14} exact " + " ".join(f"{x:5.3f}" for x in q))
rng = random.Random(3)
draws = [sample_token(rng, LOGITS, 1.0, p=0.9) for _ in range(100_000)]
print(f"{'top-p, 0.9':<14} drawn " + " ".join(f"{draws.count(i) / len(draws):5.3f}" for i in range(6)))
     T  max prob  entropy (bits)  perplexity
   0.1     1.000           0.004        1.00
  0.25     0.957           0.279        1.21
   0.5     0.771           1.071        2.10
   1.0     0.512           1.897        3.72
   2.0     0.336           2.347        5.09
   5.0     0.230           2.540        5.82
 100.0     0.170           2.585        6.00

                  the     a   cat   dog   ran   sat
T = 1          exact 0.512 0.230 0.114 0.103 0.031 0.009
top-k, k = 3   exact 0.598 0.269 0.133 0.000 0.000 0.000
top-p, 0.9     exact 0.534 0.240 0.119 0.108 0.000 0.000
top-p, 0.9     drawn 0.536 0.239 0.120 0.105 0.000 0.000

These are the figures of chapters 12 and 14, reproduced. Notice that top-p with 0.9 kept four tokens: the first three only reach a total of 0.856, short of 0.9, so a fourth is needed. A subtle point is the word "smallest" and the inequality "at least": a nucleus of 0.5 over [0.5, 0.25, 0.25] keeps exactly one token, because its mass reaches 0.5 and stops there. The last row draws 100,000 tokens through sample_token, which composes everything from milestones 1, 4 and 5 (temperature, top-k, top-p, then the categorical walk), and the frequencies match the exact row to about two decimals.

Common misconception

"Temperature 0 means no randomness, so the API should accept T = 0." Dividing by zero is undefined, and the limit of the softmax as T tends to 0 is the arg-max, so APIs that accept 0 treat it as a special case: greedy decoding. Your softmax_t raises ValueError for T ≤ 0 and is stable for T = 0.001 (where the scaled logits are in the thousands, the situation milestone 4 prepared you for). Note also that greedy decoding is not guaranteed to give the same text on every run: parallel hardware sums floating-point numbers in orders that can vary, and two logits that are nearly tied can swap places (chapter 11).

milestones.title: cross-entropy, KL, its estimators and the leash

milestones.explain:
The last milestone assembles the quantities of chapter 14. The cross-entropy H(p, q) = −∑ pi log qi is the average surprise of a model q on data that really come from p; it is the training loss of chapter 13 estimated from a sample. The KL divergence KL(p ‖ q) = ∑ pi log(pi/qi) is the part of it that the model could in principle remove: H(p, q) = H(p) + KL(p ‖ q). It is never negative (Gibbs' inequality), it is zero only when q = p, it is not symmetric, and it is infinite if q gives probability 0 to something p allows. The script prints the chapter's table for p = (0.7, 0.2, 0.1):

from solution import entropy, xent, kl

P = [0.7, 0.2, 0.1]
models = {"perfect": P, "nearly right": [0.6, 0.25, 0.15], "uniform guess": [1 / 3] * 3, "confidently wrong": [0.05, 0.05, 0.9]}
print(f"true p = {P}, entropy H(p) = {entropy(P):.4f} bits")
print(f"{'model':<18} {'H(p,q)':>8} {'KL(p||q)':>9} {'KL(q||p)':>9}")
for name, q in models.items():
    print(f"{name:<18} {xent(P, q):8.4f} {kl(P, q):9.4f} {kl(q, P):9.4f}")
print("KL(p || q) with q = [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]:", kl(P, [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]))
true p = [0.7, 0.2, 0.1], entropy H(p) = 1.1568 bits
model                H(p,q)  KL(p||q)  KL(q||p)
perfect              1.1568    0.0000    0.0000
nearly right         1.1896    0.0328    0.0348
uniform guess        1.5850    0.4282    0.4678
confidently wrong    3.9049    2.7482    2.5626
KL(p || q) with q = [0.8, 0.2, 0.0]: inf

The perfect model pays the entropy and nothing more. A confidently wrong model pays 2.75 extra bits in one direction and 2.56 in the other: the asymmetry is real, so always say which direction you mean, and notice which distribution the expectation is taken under (the first argument).

Estimating KL from samples

For a language model the exact KL(π ‖ πref) at one position is a sum over a vocabulary of 100,000 tokens, and over a whole reply it is an expectation over an astronomical number of sequences. Training code instead samples a token x from the current policy π (which was generating it anyway), looks up both models' log-probabilities for that token, and averages. John Schulman's note Approximating KL Divergence (2020) compares three single-sample estimators. Write r = πref(x)/π(x). Then

  • k1 = −ln r = ln(π/πref). Unbiased: its expectation under π is exactly the KL. But it is negative for many individual samples, even though the KL is positive, so it has high variance.
  • k2 = (ln r)2/2. Never negative and lower variance, but slightly biased.
  • k3 = (r − 1) − ln r. Unbiased and never negative. It is k1 plus the term r − 1, which has expectation zero under π because ∑x π(x)(πref(x)/π(x) − 1) = ∑ πref − ∑ π = 1 − 1 = 0, and which is negatively correlated with k1, so adding it cancels noise. Geometrically, it is the gap between the curve ln r and its tangent line at r = 1, which is why it cannot be negative.

That expectation argument can be checked exactly, with no sampling noise, by enumerating the five tokens of a small vocabulary and weighting each estimator by π(x); check.py does so and demands that k1 and k3 reproduce the exact KL to 12 digits while k2 does not. Then estimate_kl draws tokens with your categorical sampler and reports the mean and per-sample standard deviation of each:

import random
from solution import kl, estimate_kl, NATS

pi, ref = [0.40, 0.30, 0.15, 0.10, 0.05], [0.30, 0.30, 0.20, 0.10, 0.10]
print(f"\nexact KL(pi || ref) = {kl(pi, ref, NATS):.5f} nats; 20,000 sampled tokens, three estimators")
est = estimate_kl(random.Random(1), pi, ref, 20000)
for k, (m, sd) in est.items():
    print(f"  {k}: mean {m:.5f}   per-sample sd {sd:.4f}")

exact KL(pi || ref) = 0.03726 nats; 20,000 sampled tokens, three estimators
  k1: mean 0.03655   per-sample sd 0.2619
  k2: mean 0.03496   per-sample sd 0.0518
  k3: mean 0.03755   per-sample sd 0.0656

All three means are close to the exact 0.03726 nats, and k2's is a little low (its expected value is 0.0348, 7% under the truth, a bias that the 20,000 samples resolve). The column that matters is the standard deviation: a single k1 sample has a spread of 0.26, seven times the KL it estimates, while k3 has 0.066. To reach the same accuracy, k1 needs about 16 times as many samples as k3. This is why PPO and GRPO implementations that estimate their KL penalty from sampled tokens (A3, chapter 8; chapter 14) commonly use k3 rather than the raw log-ratio.

The KL leash in closed form

Reinforcement learning from human feedback tunes a policy π to maximise a reward r(y) while a penalty keeps it near the reference model: maximise Ey∼π[r(y)] − β KL(π ‖ πref). The coefficient β sets how long the leash is. For a small set of candidate replies this has an exact solution, derived in chapter 14 with a Lagrange multiplier for the constraint ∑π = 1:

π*(y) = πref(y) · exp(r(y)/β) / Z,    Z = ∑y πref(y) exp(r(y)/β).

The optimal policy is the reference reweighted by the exponentiated reward, so leash_policy is a softmax of the logits ln πref(y) + r(y)/β, which means your milestone-4 function does the work and the stable form is free. A small enough β makes r/β huge (5,000 at β = 0.001 for a reward of 5), and the naive form overflows exactly as it did in milestone 4. The check also confirms the property that A3's DPO derivation rests on: taking logs, β ln(π*(y)/πref(y)) = r(y) − β ln Z, so the reward equals β times the log-ratio plus a constant that is the same for every reply. A model's log-ratio to its reference is a reward, up to that constant, which is what lets DPO train on preference pairs without a separate reward model.

from solution import kl, leash_policy, NATS

ref, reward = [0.55, 0.25, 0.15, 0.05], [0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 5.0]
print(f"\nreference {ref}, rewards {reward}")
print(f"{'beta':>6} {'optimal policy':>30} {'E[reward]':>10} {'KL(pi||ref)':>12}")
for beta in (100.0, 10.0, 3.0, 1.0, 0.3):
    pol = leash_policy(ref, reward, beta)
    print(f"{beta:6} {str([round(x, 3) for x in pol]):>30} {sum(a * r for a, r in zip(pol, reward)):10.3f} {kl(pol, ref, NATS):12.3f}")

reference [0.55, 0.25, 0.15, 0.05], rewards [0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 5.0]
  beta                 optimal policy  E[reward]  KL(pi||ref)
 100.0    [0.546, 0.25, 0.152, 0.052]      0.815        0.000
  10.0   [0.504, 0.253, 0.168, 0.075]      0.966        0.009
   3.0    [0.378, 0.24, 0.201, 0.182]      1.550        0.141
   1.0     [0.056, 0.07, 0.114, 0.76]      4.099        1.821
   0.3           [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0]      5.000        2.994

With a strong leash (β = 100) the policy is the reference (KL 0.000). At β = 3 it has moved towards the rewarded replies, expected reward 1.55 for a KL of 0.141 nats. At β = 1 most of the mass (0.76) sits on the highest-reward reply, 1.82 nats from the reference, and at β = 0.3 everything does. If that last reply is the one a flawed reward model over-values, the leash is what limits the damage (A3, chapter 13). check.py also tests optimality directly: the objective at your policy is at least the objective at 300 random alternatives, for two values of β.
